blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 28 (Chromatography), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is chromatography? Explain why it is needed for complex mixtures, what it allows chemists to do, and name its three important types. Also define adsorption with an example. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Need: one or two components can be separated from a simple mixture by simple techniques such as filtration, distillation and solvent extraction, but complex mixtures require advanced techniques.

Chromatography: a versatile and important analytical technique that separates the individual components of a complex mixture based on their varying affinities for two different phases (a stationary phase and a mobile phase). Examples of such mixtures: dyes in blooming flowers, pollutants in a water body, medicinal extracts from plant leaves (e.g. the mixture of pigments in leaves).

Uses: it allows identification, purification and quantification of substances with high precision, so it is an efficient modern analytical tool in medicine, forensic and environmental science.

Three important types: paper chromatography (PC), thin layer chromatography (TLC) and gas chromatography (GC).

Adsorption: a surface phenomenon in which particles accumulate only on the outer surface. Example: activated charcoal adsorbs gases and impurities onto its surface, so it is used in filters and purification systems.

book_ref.quote: Chromatography is a versatile and important analytical technique

blocks.prompt: 2 Explain the roles of the stationary phase and the mobile phase in paper chromatography. What is the Rf value? Give its formula and explain why it has no unit and when it stays constant. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Stationary phase: the paper contains water combined with the cellulose of the paper; this trapped water is the stationary phase.
Mobile phase: the solvent, which soaks up the paper and moves upward past the sample spot (the solvent level is kept below the spot).

Separation: the solutes in the sample dissolve in the two phases to different extents. Components more soluble in the solvent (mobile phase) move up the paper; components that dissolve better in the water of the paper (stationary phase) do not travel far. This difference in solubility separates them; the principle is relative solubility (partition).

Rf value (retardation or retention factor):
Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent
• Rf has no unit because it is a ratio of two distances.
• The Rf value of a substance does not change under the same conditions (same solvent and same temperature), so it can be used to identify the substance.

book_ref.quote: This difference in the solubility allows the different components in the sample to be separated.

blocks.prompt: 3 A mixture of two dyes is run on paper. The solvent front is 8.0 cm from the baseline. Dye P is at 2.4 cm and dye Q at 5.6 cm. (i) Calculate the Rf value of each dye. (ii) Which dye is more soluble in the water of the paper? (iii) Where would a dye of Rf 0.45 appear on a paper whose solvent front is 6.0 cm? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Divide each spot's distance by the solvent's distance; the dye that moves less stays more in the stationary water; for (iii) multiply Rf by the solvent distance.

book_ref.quote: is calculated by dividing the distance traveled by the component with the distance travelled by the solvent.

steps: Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent
P moves less (lower Rf), so it dissolves better in the water trapped in the paper (stationary phase).
(iii) distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.45 × 6.0 cm = 2.7 cm
blocks.final_answer: Rf(P) = 0.30, Rf(Q) = 0.70; P is more soluble in the water of the paper; the Rf 0.45 dye appears 2.7 cm from the baseline.

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe how a TLC plate is prepared and how the samples are spotted and run. How are colourless components made visible? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Preparation of the plate: alumina (Al₂O₃) or silica (SiO₂) is mixed in water to make a slurry, which is spread evenly onto a glass slide. The layer is dried in an oven to make a white solid layer, the stationary phase.

Spotting and running:
• A straight baseline is drawn with pencil and ruler near the bottom of the slide.
• A spot of sample is put on the baseline with a capillary tube; more than one sample can be spotted at different places on the same slide.
• The solvent (mobile phase) is taken in a chromatography tank and the slide is dipped so that the baseline is above the solvent level.
• After the solvent has moved up to a certain height the slide is removed, the solvent front is marked and the slide is dried with a dryer.

Visualising colourless components (locating agents):
• Ninhydrin spray gives purple colour to colourless amino acids.
• Some colourless substances glow when irradiated with ultra-violet light.
• Some turn brown with iodine vapours.

book_ref.quote: In thin layer chromatography (TLC), alumina (Al₂O₃) or silica (SiO₂) is mixed in water to make slurry

blocks.prompt: 5 Explain how the polarity of substances decides how far they travel in TLC, and how the separated components are finally identified. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Two processes act together: the components dissolve in the solvent (mobile phase) and adsorb onto the aluminium oxide (stationary phase) to different extents.

• Polar substances have greater attraction for the polar solid stationary phase and are adsorbed more strongly, so they travel more slowly up the slide (small Rf).
• Non-polar substances are more soluble in the non-polar solvent, so they move further up the slide (large Rf).
This difference in adsorption and solubility separates the substances (principle: adsorption + solubility).

Identification: after the run the solvent front is marked and the slide is dried. The Rf value of each spot is calculated (Rf = distance of spot / distance of solvent) and compared with standard values; matching Rf values identify the components. Colourless spots are first made visible with a locating agent (ninhydrin, UV light or iodine vapours).

book_ref.quote: This difference allows the substances in the sample to separate.

blocks.prompt: 6 A sample is run on a TLC slide. The solvent front is 6.0 cm from the baseline and two spots appear at 1.5 cm and 4.5 cm. In the same solvent and temperature, standard Rf values are: X = 0.25, Y = 0.50, Z = 0.75. (i) Calculate the Rf of both spots. (ii) Identify the components. (iii) Which component is more polar if the stationary phase is polar? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find each Rf, match it with the standard list (valid because conditions are the same), and remember that the more polar substance is held back more.

book_ref.quote: Rf values of different coloured spots are calculated.

steps: Rf = distance of spot / distance of solvent front
Spot 1: Rf = 1.5 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.25 → matches X
Spot 2: Rf = 4.5 cm / 6.0 cm = 0.75 → matches Z
Rf values do not change under the same solvent and temperature, so the matches are valid.
X (Rf 0.25) is held back more by the polar stationary phase, so X is more polar.
blocks.final_answer: Rf = 0.25 (X) and 0.75 (Z); the sample contains X and Z; X is the more polar component.

blocks.prompt: 7 Describe the applications of thin layer chromatography. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Identification: TLC identifies unknown compounds by comparing their Rf values with standard known values.
2. Purity: the purity of a substance can be checked by TLC.
3. Reaction progress: TLC shows whether reactants are being consumed or products are being made.
4. Pharmaceutical and food industry: the purity of drugs and the presence of preservatives, colourants and sweeteners in food can be checked.
5. Environment: TLC detects pollutants, pesticides and toxic substances in soil, water, food and air.
6. Forensic science: it identifies drugs, post-blast debris, blood, sweat and semen at a crime scene.

book_ref.quote: In pharmaceutical and food industry, purity of drugs and presence of preservatives

blocks.prompt: 8 Explain the limitations of thin layer chromatography. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Mainly qualitative: TLC can only give an idea about the amount of a substance, so it is not an accurate and precise quantitative technique.
2. Poor resolution for close Rf values: TLC cannot clearly separate compounds having close Rf values, so resolution of spots is not always high and sharp.
3. Small scale only: only small amounts of sample can be applied and analysed, so it is not suitable for large-scale separation.
4. Low reproducibility: the technique is sensitive to humidity, temperature and cleanliness of the working environment, which reduces reproducibility.

book_ref.quote: In TLC, only small amounts of sample can be applied and analysed.

blocks.prompt: 9 Explain how the components of a mixture are separated inside the column of a gas chromatograph. What are retention time and a chromatogram? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Phases: the stationary phase is a non-volatile, long-chain, non-polar hydrocarbon liquid of high boiling point bonded to small particles of silica (SiO₂) or alumina (Al₂O₃); the mobile phase is an inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen.

Separation: the vaporised sample is carried by the carrier gas through a long coiled column packed with tiny silica particles of large surface area, over which separation occurs. Non-polar substances interact more with the non-polar liquid of the stationary phase, so they are carried through the column more slowly. Substances that interact more strongly move slower while others move faster, which separates them (principle: gas-liquid partition).

Chromatogram: as the separated substances exit the column, they pass through a detector which identifies and records them as peaks on a graph called a chromatogram.

Retention time: the time taken by a substance to pass through the column; the detector records it for each component.

book_ref.quote: The non-polar substances in the mixture have greater interaction with non-polar liquid

blocks.prompt: 10 Explain how gas chromatography is used as a quantitative technique to find the composition of a mixture of three esters A, B and C. When is peak height used instead of peak area? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
GC has high sensitivity, good resolution, fast analysis and accurate quantification; it is a quantitative technique.

1. The peaks on the chromatogram are first identified (each component gives its own peak).
2. The area of each peak is measured. The peaks are similar to triangles, so:
   Area of a peak = ½ × base × height
3. The area of each peak gives the proportion of that component:
   % of A = peak area of A / (sum of peak areas of A, B and C) × 100
   and similarly for B and C.

Peak height: if the peaks are very narrow or have similar base widths, peak height is used instead of area to estimate the proportion of the components.

book_ref.quote: GC is also a quantitative technique.

blocks.prompt: 11 A mixture of three esters A, B and C gives a gas chromatogram with triangular peaks: A (base 2.0 mm, height 6.0 mm), B (base 2.0 mm, height 9.0 mm), C (base 3.0 mm, height 10.0 mm). Calculate the percentage of each ester in the mixture. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find each peak area as ½ × base × height, add them, then take each area as a percentage of the total.

book_ref.quote: The peaks are similar to triangles, therefore, the area of peak can be calculated by the following formula.

blocks.prompt: 12 Describe the applications of gas chromatography in industry, forensic science, the food industry, clinical work and sports. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
1. Industry: GC is vital for quality control and environmental protection; petrochemical plants use it to analyse the composition of fuels and to detect trace amounts of organic pollutants in environmental samples.
2. Forensic science: it is frequently used for blood alcohol content (BAC) tests and to detect illegal drugs, poisons or performance-enhancing substances in biological samples. (Example: food in the Nian Bin case was tested by GC, which proved no poison had been mixed.)
3. Food and beverage industry: it ensures consistency and safety, detecting spoilage by identifying metabolic byproducts of bacteria or fungi before they are visible, and analyses the aromatic profiles of perfumes, essential oils and flavourings.
4. Clinical and pharmaceutical: it diagnoses metabolic disorders by analysing compounds in a patient's breath or urine, and tests the purity of newly synthesised drugs so that no harmful residual solvents or impurities remain.
5. Sports: it checks the presence of steroids in competing athletes and tests the components of fuel used in car racing.

book_ref.quote: In the industrial sector, GC is vital for quality control and environmental protection.

blocks.prompt: 13 State the advantages and the limitations of gas chromatography. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Advantages:
• High sensitivity, good resolution, fast analysis and accurate quantification.
• Mixtures of gases can easily be separated at room temperature.
• It is a quantitative technique: peak areas give the proportion of each component.

Limitations:
1. GC works only for volatile (easily vaporised) substances.
2. Samples must be thermally stable; compounds that decompose at high temperatures cannot be used.
3. Large biomolecules like proteins and polymers cannot be analysed because they do not vaporise easily.
4. Instruments and maintenance costs for GC are high.

book_ref.quote: GC works only for volatile (easily vaporised) substances.

blocks.prompt: 14 Compare paper chromatography, thin layer chromatography and gas chromatography with respect to principle, mobile phase, stationary phase and speed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: The three types compare as shown in the table. Paper chromatography separates by relative solubility between the solvent and the water in the paper; TLC by adsorption on silica/alumina together with solubility in the solvent; GC by partition between a carrier gas and a non-volatile liquid in a coiled column.

book_ref.quote: Comparison of three types of chromatography
